title: Should he teach?
hookLine: he hesitates; Brahma Sahampati asks him to teach; he sees people like lotuses near the surface (MN 26)

lines: IT SOUNDED LIKE A GREETING CARD.
cards: Have you ever understood something so deeply that you didn't know how to say it? Maybe you went through something hard, a loss, an illness, a recovery, and came out the other side knowing something.
Then someone asked you about it, you opened your mouth, and it sounded like a greeting card. Some things don't fit into words very well. The Buddha has found what he was looking for.
Now comes a question that's easy to skip past: should he tell anyone at all?

teach.b: The Buddha tells this himself. What I've found, he thinks, is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, subtle, beyond mere reasoning. And people love their attachments; they delight in them.
For people like that, this would be hard to see. If I taught it, and others didn't understand, that would only be wearying for me. So his mind leans toward not teaching.
Then, the sutta says, a great god, Brahma Sahampati, realizes what's happening. The world will be lost, he thinks, if the awakened one stays silent.
In the time it takes a strong man to stretch out his bent arm, the god leaves his heaven and appears before the Buddha.
He kneels, raises his joined hands, and pleads. Let the Blessed One teach.

teach.h: A LITTLE DUST IN THEIR EYES.
teach.b: There are beings with only a little dust in their eyes, losing out because they haven't heard. Some will understand.
So the Buddha looks out over the world with the eye of an awakened one, and what he sees is a lotus pond.
Some lotuses are still deep under the water. Some have grown right up to the surface. And some stand clear above it, untouched by the water.
People are like that: some with much dust in their eyes, some with little, some ready right now. And he decides. Open are the doors to the deathless, he says, for those who have ears.
Not everyone is ready. But some are, and for them, it's worth it.

how: In the Pali telling, Brahma Sahampati's request is the turning point that sets the teaching in motion, and in some traditions a formal request to teach is made to a teacher before a dharma talk, echoing this moment.

o: a sacred fig leaf used in offerings
a lotus flower, rising from the water
a pool of still water for washing

games.q: what's inside the moment — tap the pairs.
p: knelt and asked him to teach
a little dust in their eyes

s: the Buddha first thought his teaching would be easy to grasp
he found it deep, subtle and hard to see, and his mind leaned toward not teaching.
in the sutta, a god asks the Buddha to teach
Brahma Sahampati kneels and pleads: some have only a little dust in their eyes.
the Buddha saw that everyone was equally ready
he saw lotuses at every depth: some deep, some near the surface, some already above it.

games.q: you've found something deep and hard to put into words. a god kneels before you: some will understand. what do you do?
o: stay silent: they won't get it.
look out over the world, and decide to teach.
games.why: he surveys the world and sees people like lotuses at every depth. the doors to the deathless are open, he says, and he decides to teach.

practice: Picture a still pond, green stems reaching up from the mud, and pick one lotus bud to watch as it rises slowly through the dark water toward the light.
It breaks the surface, stands in the air with drops of water rolling off, and opens, petal by petal, at its own speed. If your mind wanders, return to the pond.

wordCard.voice: Paduma. The lotuses in the Buddha's vision of the pond: some still under water, some risen, like people with more or less dust in their eyes.

orig.note: Pali: lotus (Sanskrit padma), one of the flowers in the Buddha's vision of the pond.

carryVoice: Your line: some are ready. The doors to the deathless are open. Fifty-nine days in.

sources.ref: Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26): the hesitation and the request
